challenges.title: A free line on the form
challenges.scene: Participants read one truthful norm message (what others did or approved of, framed positively or negatively), then reported whether a die roll matched a number they privately chose. Matches paid a bonus; lies were undetectable.
challenges.question: How likely is it that at least one message reduced cheating?

forecast.claim: At least one of the four honesty messages reduced cheating compared with no message.

challenges.answerTitle: None of the four messages changed behavior
challenges.explain: The pre-registered, high-powered study found null effects with tight confidence intervals for all four messages. A follow-up showed the messages did not change perceived norms.
challenges.implication: Before adding an honesty statement to expense or reporting forms, test whether it actually shifts employees' beliefs about the norm.
challenges.boundary: One-line messages before a die-reporting game with undetectable lies; other norm interventions may behave differently.

follow.q: Why did the messages fail?
follow.a: A follow-up experiment found the messages did not change norm perceptions, so there was no belief shift to move behavior.

follow.q: Did anyone react to the message?
follow.a: Many participants misremembered the message in a way that supported cheating, and this group cheated significantly more.

follow.q: Did the framing matter?
follow.a: No. Neither empirical vs normative content nor positive vs negative framing produced an effect; none of the four worked.

study.n: High-powered sample (size not confirmed in published text read)

evidence.quote: We find compelling null effects with tight confidence intervals showing that none of the norm-nudge interventions worked.

challenges.title: "Everyone does it," they say
challenges.scene: A sales team knows its commission scheme can be gamed. In a survey, the people who misreport are also the ones most likely to say most colleagues misreport.
challenges.question: What best explains the link between this belief and misreporting?
options: The belief is accurate information that drives lying
Temptation distorts the belief to justify lying
The belief and lying are unrelated
Honest employees hold this belief most strongly

dag.alt: Profit from lying feeds both the belief that most people lie and lying itself; the belief-to-lying arrow may be partly reversed.

challenges.answerTitle: Temptation reshapes beliefs to excuse lying
challenges.explain: Results fit a model in which conditional norm-followers strategically distort their beliefs to justify self-serving behavior. Widespread honesty signaled disapproval of lying, but widespread lying did not signal approval.
challenges.implication: Do not treat "everyone games it" survey answers as facts; check them against actual compliance data and publish what peers really do.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized experiment where lying paid money; beliefs concerned other participants, not long-term colleagues.

follow.q: Which beliefs were distorted?
follow.a: The paper studies two: empirical beliefs (what others do) and normative beliefs (what others approve of), and shows when and which are distorted.

follow.q: Which signal is hardest to explain away?
follow.a: Widespread honest behavior. People read it as a strong sign that lying is disapproved of; widespread lying was not read as approval.

follow.q: Who distorts beliefs?
follow.a: Conditional norm-followers: people who follow a norm only when they believe it applies, and who shade those beliefs when lying pays.

evidence.quote: We investigate self-serving belief distortion about dominant norms of honesty.
in which conditional norm-followers strategically distort their beliefs to justify self-serving behavior.
widespread honest behavior is a strong indicator of disapproval of lying (and thus that a norm of honesty is followed), but the opposite does not hold.

challenges.title: The open dashboard problem
challenges.scene: Penn students played repeated rounds of a charity game: give to, take from, or leave a donation. One group could see peers' past choices; another could not.
challenges.question: By about how much did donations fall when peers' choices were visible?

estimate.label: Drop in donations vs no visibility

challenges.answerTitle: Donations fell about 20% with visibility alone
challenges.explain: With observation alone, participants took an additional 21.9 ECUs and donations fell by about 20% compared with no observation. People copied bad examples but ignored good ones.
challenges.implication: Before publishing peer compliance dashboards, build real shared identity in the team, or bad examples will spread faster than good ones.
challenges.boundary: Lab game with Penn students in small groups, no sanctions; social proximity was a minimal shared-identity cue.

follow.q: Did shared identity help?
follow.a: Yes. With a minimal social-proximity cue, extra taking fell to 7.5 ECUs, and seeing peers give raised donations by about 0.20 ECU per ECU given.

follow.q: How strongly did people copy bad behavior?
follow.a: Without proximity, each ECU a peer took cut a participant's own donation by about 0.24 ECU. Seeing peers give had no significant effect.

follow.q: Were the groups different at the start?
follow.a: No. Initial takers were 45%, 44% and 42% across conditions (p = 0.703), so the gap emerged from watching peers.

challenges.title: Which behavior spreads faster?
challenges.scene: In an experiment, people saw what peers had chosen before making their own pro-social or anti-social choices. The design also varied how socially close those peers were.
challenges.question: Which two findings did the study report?
options: Anti-social behavior was more contagious than pro-social
Closeness amplified bad behavior's spread more than good
Pro-social behavior was the more contagious
Closeness spread only good behavior
Anti-social people resisted anti-social peers most
challenges.answerTitle: Bad behavior spreads more, especially among close peers
challenges.explain: Anti-social behavior was generally more contagious than pro-social behavior, and social proximity amplified the contagion of anti-social behavior more strongly than that of pro-social behavior.
challenges.implication: Address visible misconduct inside tight-knit teams quickly; close peers copy it more readily than they copy good conduct.
challenges.boundary: One experiment with stylized pro- and anti-social choices; real workplace misconduct was not observed.

follow.q: Who was most affected?
follow.a: Anti-social individuals were the most susceptible to contagion from other anti-social peers.

follow.q: Does closeness always make things worse?
follow.a: Not always. In a later repeated-group study (Bicchieri, Dimant, Gächter & Nosenzo 2022), a minimal shared-identity cue led people to copy good examples too, halting the erosion of compliance.

follow.q: What is the finding meant to inform?
follow.a: Norm-based interventions: the paper argues its results help design policies that encourage pro-social and reduce anti-social behavior.

evidence.quote: we find that anti-social behavior is generally more contagious than pro-social behavior.
social proximity amplifies the contagion of anti-social behavior more strongly than the contagion of pro-social behavior.
Anti-social individuals are also most susceptible to the behavioral contagion of other anti-social peers.
With social proximity, participants conform to both types of observed behaviors, thus halting the erosion of compliance.

challenges.title: Small fine, which message?
challenges.scene: In a trust game, researchers added a weak penalty for returning too little, alone or with a message about what most others do or what most think is right. The cost of complying also varied.
challenges.question: Which combination raised reciprocity?
options: Weak penalty alone
Norm message alone
Penalty plus "most think it's right," cheap compliance
Penalty plus "most others comply," costly compliance
challenges.answerTitle: Penalty plus normative message, only when compliance is cheap
challenges.explain: Neither weak punishment nor norm information alone increased reciprocity. Together, weak punishment and normative information raised it when compliance was cheap; with costly compliance, punishment plus empirical information could backfire.
challenges.implication: When a sanction is modest and compliance is costly, do not justify it with "everyone complies"; explain why the rule is right.
challenges.boundary: Lab trust game with a weak penalty and generic norm messages; strong sanctions and real team norms were not tested.

follow.q: Why did the costly case backfire?
follow.a: Additional experiments attribute it to the punishment being perceived as unjustified, at least by some people.

follow.q: Did the penalty work on its own?
follow.a: No. In isolation, neither weak punishment nor empirical or normative information increased reciprocal behavior.

follow.q: How many conditions were tested?
follow.a: Six, systematically combining whether weak punishment existed with no norm information, empirical information or normative information.

study.n: Six conditions; size not confirmed in published text read

evidence.quote: We show that in isolation, neither weak punishment nor empirical/normative information increase prosocial, reciprocal behavior.
reciprocity significantly increases when normative information and weak punishment are combined, but only when compliance is relatively cheap.
When compliance is more costly, we find that the combination of punishment and generic empirical information about others' conformity can have detrimental effects.
this negative effect can be attributed to the punishment being perceived as unjustified, at least in some individuals.
Across six conditions, we systematically vary the combination of the existence of weak punishment and norm information.

challenges.title: Who gets reported for bribery?
challenges.scene: US adults read about a coworker accepting a bribe and chose how likely they were to report it. The bribe either created inequity or restored equity; half also saw norm information.
challenges.question: Rank the four cases from highest to lowest reporting probability.
options: Inequity, with norm information
Inequity, no norm information
Equity, with norm information
Equity, no norm information
challenges.answerTitle: Inequity and norm information both raised reporting
challenges.explain: Norm information raised reporting from 73.3% to 82.8% when the bribe created inequity (P < 0.005) and from 57.9% to 67.2% when it restored equity (P = 0.074).
challenges.implication: Give investigators explicit sanction guidelines; short norm statements and the perceived fairness of the gain shift how harshly they judge.

follow.q: Did the behavioral study agree?
follow.a: Yes. Lies that created inequity drew 52.8% of the maximum punishment vs 43.6% for lies that achieved equity (P < 0.001).

follow.q: Does the size of the lie matter?
follow.a: Yes. The smallest lie drew 44.7% of maximum punishment, and each larger step added about 10 percentage points.

follow.q: When do norm messages work best?
follow.a: Study 3 found norm perceptions are malleable and norm-nudges are most effective when existing norms are ambiguous.

challenges.title: Just let colleagues see it
challenges.scene: To boost charity giving, an experiment let another person observe each donation decision. In some versions the observer simply watched, with no rewards or consequences attached.
challenges.question: What did being watched, with nothing attached, do to giving?
options: Raised giving sharply
Little positive effect; it could even backfire
Raised giving only among the best-paid
No effect of any kind
challenges.answerTitle: Watching alone did little and could backfire
challenges.explain: Observability alone had very little positive effect and could even backfire, a pattern the authors trace to inequality aversion. Making norms more salient reduced the backfire and raised pro-social behavior.
challenges.implication: Do not rely on visibility alone in giving or compliance drives; pair it with a clear statement of what is expected.
challenges.boundary: Experimental charity-giving games; observers were study participants, not colleagues with ongoing relationships.

follow.q: Why would being watched backfire?
follow.a: The authors find that inequality aversion drives the backfiring of observability.

follow.q: What fixed it?
follow.a: Increasing the salience of norms mitigated the unintended consequences and increased pro-social behavior.

follow.q: Do people care about being observed at all?
follow.a: Yes. Individuals were sensitive to the observability of their actions; observation alone just rarely moved behavior in the intended direction.

study.n: Not confirmed in published text read

evidence.quote: individuals are sensitive to the observability of their actions
observability alone has very little positive effect and can even backfire
inequality aversion drives the observed backfiring of observability

challenges.title: Whose example do you pick?
challenges.scene: Before a game where lying paid, US online participants chose whose information to see: a peer reporting more lenient behavior or views on lying, or a stricter one. No political labels were shown.

challenges.explain: Without identity cues, the share of lenient (above-median) information chosen was 54.61% for peers' behavior and 54.53% for peers' views, a self-serving bias in source selection.
challenges.implication: When employees pick their own benchmarks or peer examples, default them to representative norm data instead.

follow.q: Did political identity change the choice?

follow.q: How large were the samples?
follow.a: Two experiments: 1,945 participants who chose their sources and 2,414 who were assigned information.

challenges.title: Sharing what you don't believe
challenges.scene: In a multi-round sharing task, participants chose whether to share factual news or conspiracy theories, including ones they knew were false. The social feedback each kind of post earned varied.
challenges.question: What drove sharing of conspiracy theories people knew were false?
options: Inattention: they missed that the content was false
Expected and received social engagement
Low digital literacy among sharers
Nothing; people shared only what they believed
challenges.answerTitle: Expected engagement drove sharing of known falsehoods
challenges.explain: Across a pilot and three preregistered experiments, people expected conspiracy theories to draw more engagement than factual news, and shared more of them when they got more feedback, even knowing they were false.
challenges.implication: Do not reward internal posts by raw engagement; recognize accuracy and sourcing, especially when reorganization rumors circulate.
challenges.boundary: Experiments with a simulated sharing task and conspiracy content; internal company channels and real reputations were not studied.

follow.q: Did people care about accuracy at all?
follow.a: Yes, but in addition to accuracy, people seemed to value social engagement, and traded one off against the other.

follow.q: How fast did feedback matter?
follow.a: People were very sensitive to feedback in the multi-round task: more feedback for conspiracy posts than for factual news raised conspiracy sharing.

follow.q: How was this tested?
follow.a: A pilot study and three preregistered experiments, reported in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

challenges.title: Cards on top of cash
challenges.scene: A program paid US veterans cash to return unused opioid pills. Researchers randomly added two reminder cards built on timely reminders, planning prompts and loss framing.
challenges.question: How likely is it that the cards cut the cost per pill returned?

forecast.claim: Adding the reminder cards lowered the program's cost per pill returned.

challenges.answerTitle: Cards raised returns and lowered cost per pill
challenges.explain: The cards increased both the likelihood that patients returned unused pills and the number returned, and lowered cost per pill returned and per participant who returned pills.
challenges.implication: Before raising an incentive, test cheap, well-timed reminders that help people act on the incentive they already have.
challenges.boundary: US veterans in one cash buyback program for opioid pills; the cards added to, not replaced, the cash incentive.

follow.q: What did the cards do?
follow.a: They combined timely reminders, implementation prompts that help people plan the return, and loss framing of the cash on offer.

follow.q: Did more people return pills, or just more pills?
follow.a: Both. The cards raised the likelihood of returning unused pills and the number of pills returned.

follow.q: How strong is the design?
follow.a: It was a pre-registered field experiment with US veterans, published in Health Economics.

challenges.title: Why won't they cooperate?
challenges.scene: Across 15 behavioral experiments with over 8,600 people, participants decided how much to help, harm or cooperate with others who supported or opposed Donald Trump.
challenges.question: What mainly explained weaker cooperation across the political divide?
options: Grim expectations that the other side won't cooperate
Genuine unwillingness to cooperate with opponents
Stronger love for one's own side
Too little information about the other side
challenges.answerTitle: Pessimistic expectations, not unwillingness, drove the gap
challenges.explain: The intergroup conflict was attributed to grim expectations about the opposing faction's cooperativeness, not actual unwillingness to cooperate. Out-group hate appeared in behavior; in-group love appeared in perceptions.
challenges.implication: In politically mixed teams, share evidence that colleagues on the other side do cooperate before launching joint projects.
challenges.boundary: US polarization around Donald Trump in incentivized experiments, compared with other identities; ongoing coworker relationships were not studied.

follow.q: Did nudges close the gap?
follow.a: No. Defaults and norm-nudges improved prosociality but were ineffective in closing the polarization gap.

follow.q: Is love or hate the stronger force?
follow.a: It depends on the domain: in-group love showed up in perceptions, while out-group hate showed up in how people helped, harmed and cooperated.

follow.q: How large is the evidence base?
follow.a: Five preregistered studies with 15 well-powered experiments and over 8,600 participants, compared with other political and nonpolitical identities.

evidence.quote: which can be attributed to one's grim expectations regarding cooperativeness of the opposing faction, rather than one's actual unwillingness to cooperate.

challenges.title: Pick the middle or a side?
challenges.scene: A representative US sample played a strategic game after seeing how others behaved: tightly clustered, widely spread, or split into two extreme camps.
challenges.question: In the split, polarized setting, what did most people do?
options: Chose the safe middle option
Chose an extreme option despite strategic risk
Copied the average behavior
Behaved as they did in tight settings
challenges.answerTitle: Most picked extremes, accepting strategic risk
challenges.explain: In polarized environments, most people preferred extreme actions that exposed them to considerable strategic risk over intermediate actions that minimized it. Loose norms produced more varied behavior.
challenges.implication: Report the spread of team behavior, not only the average; a split norm pulls people toward one camp or the other.
challenges.boundary: Experimental strategic game with a representative US sample; real team norms and productivity were not measured.

follow.q: What do tight, loose and polarized mean?
follow.a: Tight means low variance in others' behavior, loose means high variance, and polarized means u-shaped behavior clustered at two extremes.

follow.q: Whose behavior is hardest to predict?
follow.a: In loose and polarized environments, personal traits and values played a larger role in what people actually did.

follow.q: Why look beyond the average?
follow.a: Organizations increasingly use descriptive norms to nudge behavior; the authors show the whole distribution of peer behavior, not just its mean, shapes reactions.
